design_detail: Secondary analysis of two independent US national cross-sectional surveys pooled into one data set: the National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey (NLAES, 1991–1992) and the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC, 2001–2002), both sponsored by NIAAA, with Census Bureau fieldwork and the same AUDADIS-IV interview. US-born respondents aged 18–57 (N=53,238) were grouped into five 10-year birth cohorts (born 1934–1943 to 1974–1983). Three 'telescoping' landmarks were reconstructed from ages recalled at a single interview: age at first drink, time from first drink to onset of DSM-IV alcohol dependence, and time from dependence onset to first alcohol treatment. Analyses: within-cohort comparisons of mean times (t tests), life tables with log-rank tests, and Cox proportional hazards models with cohort-by-gender and cohort-by-gender-by-time interactions, weighted for both complex sample designs (SUDAAN). A general-population sample, not a treatment sample.
can_establish: For US-born adults aged 18–57 in two national household surveys, how the recalled timing of first drink, onset of alcohol dependence and first alcohol treatment differed between men and women and between birth cohorts, and whether the sex pattern reported from treatment samples (later first drink but faster progression to dependence and to treatment in women) shows up in a general-population sample.
cannot_establish: Whether the timing differences are real rather than products of recalling ages years or decades later (nothing was recorded as it happened); why men and women differ (biological sex and gender roles are not separated, and the authors' explanation of cohort convergence by changing norms was not tested); how fast people progress once they are on the way to dependence as distinct from whether they become dependent at all (the survival and hazard analyses among all drinkers combine the two); and anything about people over 57, people born outside the US, people outside the households and group quarters sampled, or people who died before the surveys.

sample.recruitment: General-population sample: two US national multistage probability surveys of households and group quarters, interviewed face to face by trained lay interviewers; response rates 90% (NLAES) and 81% (NESARC); no person took part in both surveys (Method › Sources of Data, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: US-born respondents aged 18–57. Excluded: people older than 57 (to limit the effect of alcohol-related deaths) and people born outside the US (to limit changes in cohort make-up from immigration) (Method › Sources of Data, 2nd paragraph). Lifetime drinkers were people who had ever had more than 12 drinks (Method › Measures). The 258 people whose first treatment came before dependence onset were left out of the treatment analysis (Table 1 footnote a).
sample.demographics: Unweighted: 23,113 men and 30,125 women (Table 1). Cohorts 2–4 contribute respondents from both surveys, interviewed 10 years apart; cohort 1 comes only from NESARC (aged 18–27) and cohort 5 only from NLAES (aged 48–57) (Method › Sources of Data, 4th paragraph). Race and ethnicity, income, education and urbanicity were covariates, but their distributions are not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one interview per person). Item-level missing data are not reported, and the analysed numbers differ between Table 1 and the figures and Table 2 without explanation (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: A general-population sample, unlike the treatment samples in which telescoping was first described. Survivors only: capping age at 57 limits but does not remove the loss of people with severe dependence who died young, a loss that grows with cohort age. Each cohort is seen at different ages (cohort 1 only at 18–27, cohort 5 only at 48–57), so the youngest cohort can contribute only early transitions to dependence and treatment, and cohort, age and survey year are partly bound together. Treatment is uncommon (24.6% of people with dependence had ever had any alcohol treatment, per the Discussion), so the treatment comparisons rest on 3,056 treated people, including only 72 and 65 women in cohorts 1 and 5.

exposure.measurement: The groups compared are men and women (the paper uses 'gender' throughout and does not separate biological sex from gender roles) and birth cohort (five 10-year groups). The landmark ages were all self-reported at a single AUDADIS-IV interview: age at first drink (people counted at risk from age 5, the youngest age the surveys accepted), age at onset of DSM-IV alcohol dependence (three or more of seven criteria clustering within one year) and age at first alcohol treatment. All timing was recalled, none recorded as it happened.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed: quantity and frequency of drinking are not in the models. The paper does not spell out whether 'initiation' means the first drink or the point of having had more than 12 drinks; the Figure 1 legend counts years to the first drink.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: other drug use and other drug use disorders are neither described nor adjusted for.

comparison.controls: Men compared with women within each birth cohort; successive birth cohorts compared with each other, separately in men and in women.
comparison.matching: None. The Cox models adjusted for survey (NLAES vs NESARC), race/ethnicity, income, education and urbanicity, and for age at first drink in the dependence and treatment models; whether age itself stayed in the final models is stated inconsistently (see reporting issues). Birth cohort was a five-level categorical variable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of alcohol problems, childhood adversity, conduct problems, other psychiatric disorders, body size and composition, amount drunk and other drug use were not included. Income and education were measured at the interview, years after many of the events being timed, so they may be consequences of drinking rather than prior characteristics.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV (structured lay-administered interview with DSM-IV criteria); the authors cite good to excellent reliability and validity of its alcohol diagnoses (refs 19–21). 'First treatment' is described as first engagement with treatment, or any type of alcohol treatment; which services counted is not defined in this paper.
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability of the diagnosis is cited; the reliability of the recalled onset ages is not reported. The authors' recall check compared, within each birth cohort, the prevalence of dependence that began at age 25 or later between the two surveys (no difference found; Discussion, 6th paragraph); it tests forgetting of later-onset episodes over 10 years, not whether men and women recall timing differently.
outcomes.operationalization: Telescoping was defined as a later age at first drink in women together with shorter times from first drink to dependence and from dependence to first treatment (Introduction, 3rd paragraph). Times were analysed three ways: (a) mean times among people who had the event (Table 1; the authors warn these are distorted because older people have had more time); (b) survival curves among everyone at risk (all lifetime drinkers for dependence, all people with dependence for treatment), censored at current age; (c) hazard ratios for men against women by cohort, with two-way and three-way interactions.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The three landmarks were tested with t tests in 18 cells, log-rank tests for each cohort and for adjacent cohorts in each sex, and Cox main effects and two-way and three-way interactions: several dozen tests without correction (editors' count).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (structured interview; interviewers knew respondents' sex).

analysis.effect_sizes: Hazard ratios, men compared with women, with 95% CIs (Table 2). First drink: cohort 1 1.50 (1.37–1.64), cohort 2 1.50 (1.43–1.57), cohort 3 1.62 (1.55–1.70), cohort 4 2.01 (1.91–2.12), cohort 5 2.19 (2.01–2.39). Time from first drink to dependence, among lifetime drinkers: 1.56 (1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02), 1.71 (1.34–2.20). Time from dependence to first treatment, among people with dependence: 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58), 1.38 (0.84–2.26). Interactions (Table 2 footnotes): first drink, two-way F=16.7, df=4, p<0.01, three-way F=0.10, df=6, p=0.84; dependence, two-way F=2.51, df=4, p=0.04, three-way F=54.1, df=6, p<0.01; treatment, two-way F=0.92, df=4, p=0.46, three-way F=0.02, df=6, p=0.98. Mean times among people with the event (Table 1), men vs women overall: first drink 17.8 vs 19.0 years; first drink to dependence 5.8 vs 5.6 years (ratio 1.04, not significant); dependence to first treatment 7.0 vs 6.1 years (ratio 1.15, p<0.05). The coefficients of the three-way interactions are not shown.
analysis.covariates: Survey, race/ethnicity, income, education and urbanicity in all models; age at first drink in the dependence and treatment models; age reported as not retained in the Methods but as controlled in the Results and in the Table 2 footnote. Cohort, age and survey year are close to collinear (age is roughly survey year minus birth year), so cohort effects are identified only through within-cohort age spread and the two survey years; the paper does not discuss this.
analysis.selective_reporting: The direction of the three-way interaction on which the abstract's main new claim rests (men faster to dependence, especially in younger cohorts) is 'data not shown'; the 5-year-cohort sensitivity analyses and the survey-by-survey post hoc analyses are described only as similar, without numbers.
analysis.power: The authors state that the treatment analyses lacked power to detect small cohort differences because treatment is rare (24.6% of people with dependence ever treated); each cohort had at least 4,600 people (Discussion, 6th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this general-population sample, women reported a later first drink than men in every cohort (overall means 19.0 vs 17.8 years; the gap shrank from 3.0 years in the oldest cohort to 0.4 in the youngest), and the men-to-women hazard ratio for a first drink fell from 2.19 to 1.50. Among all lifetime drinkers, men had a higher hazard of alcohol dependence in every cohort (HR 1.36–1.79), and among people with dependence men had a higher hazard of first treatment (significant in cohorts 2 and 3, HR 1.55 and 1.42). Among the people who did become dependent, however, mean time from first drink to dependence was about the same in men and women overall (5.8 vs 5.6 years) and shorter in women in cohort 2 (3.7 vs 4.2 years, p=0.02); among people treated, women's mean time from dependence to first treatment was shorter overall (6.1 vs 7.0 years, p<0.05) and in the oldest cohort (19.4 vs 23.5 years).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports little evidence of telescoping in women and says a three-way interaction suggests men have a shorter time to dependence, especially in younger cohorts; the conclusion states that "A telescoping effect is not evident in the general population" (Abstract, Conclusions). Gaps: (1) in the survival and hazard analyses 'time to dependence' is computed among all lifetime drinkers, so a higher male hazard largely reflects men's higher chance of ever becoming dependent, not faster progression among those who do; the mean times among people who became dependent, which correspond to what treatment-sample studies measured, show no male advantage and a shorter time in women in one cohort; (2) the direction of the three-way interaction behind 'especially in younger cohorts' is not shown, and the youngest cohort can only contribute transitions completed by age 27; (3) the Discussion (2nd paragraph) says that, on mean times as well as survival curves, women had neither a shorter time to dependence nor a shorter time to treatment, which Table 1 contradicts in part; (4) all timing is recalled, and the recall check does not test differences in recall between men and women; (5) the explanation of convergence by changing gender norms is offered as consistent with other research, and the authors say they know of no formal test of it. The limitations paragraph is candid about recall and power, and 'full' or 'complete' telescoping is the wording used in the Discussion and Conclusions.

timeline.event: Telescoping first described in women in treatment for alcohol problems (Piazza, Vrbka and Yeager, 1989; ref. 1 of this paper).
Project MATCH treatment sample: telescoping of drinking landmarks in women compared with men (cited by Keyes et al. as ref. 4).
Women entering treatment for opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence progressed faster to treatment (Hernandez-Avila, Rounsaville and Kranzler, 2004; ref. 3 of this paper).

Review of women's treatment entry and outcome states as established that women progress faster from use to regular use to first treatment (alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence), citing treatment samples and one population survey (Dawson, 1996); in that paragraph the label of a most reproducible finding belongs to women's vulnerability to adverse medical and social consequences, not to faster progression.

This study: first test in two pooled US general-population surveys; women later to first drink, men higher hazards of dependence and treatment; mean times among people with the event similar or shorter in women.
Review cites this study as the population-based analysis that did not replicate telescoping and explains the discrepancy by sample (treatment vs population).
Critique of the telescoping concept summarizes this study as finding no telescoping in the general population and recommends discarding the term.

replication.where_it_stands: Telescoping was described in treatment samples, which this paper cites (refs 1–6), and this general-population analysis did not find the full pattern; later reviews on this round's list (mchugh_2018, marks_2018) treat it as the main general-population counter-evidence and explain the difference by sample. Whether telescoping is a feature of women's drinking careers or of who reaches treatment, and when, remains open, and the speed-versus-probability point in this card's interpretation gap is not raised in either review. No prospective cohort designed to test telescoping is cited in this paper.

Both surveys were sponsored by NIAAA, one of the funders. No commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young men and women followed from before their first drink with repeated interviews (or linked records) that record drinking, dependence criteria and treatment as they happen, analysed with methods that separate the chance of ever becoming dependent from the speed of progression among those who do (for example mixture-cure or competing-risks survival models), with measures of body composition, gender roles and access to treatment so that sex and gender can be told apart.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National probability frames of households and group quarters suit a general-population question, but the analysis keeps only US-born people aged 18–57 who survived to interview, which removes the oldest people and early deaths from severe dependence.
Multistage probability samples; the two surveys' weights and design variables were combined and analysed in SUDAAN.

53,238 people and at least 4,603 per cohort, but the treatment comparisons rest on 3,056 treated people (65–72 women in cohorts 1 and 5), and the authors say they lacked power for small treatment differences.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Survey designs described by reference, sex and cohort counts given; no table of race, income or education by sex or cohort, and 'treatment' is not defined.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Analysed numbers differ between Table 1 and the figures and Table 2 (38,812 vs 38,309 drinkers; 7,752 vs 8,564 with dependence), and the handling of missing ages is not described.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: DSM-IV alcohol dependence from the AUDADIS-IV, with cited reliability; but the measures analysed are onset ages recalled at one interview, up to decades later, whose reliability is not reported.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Same instrument and diagnostic rules in both surveys and for all respondents.

Weighted survival analysis with censoring is appropriate for onset data, but hazards among everyone at risk combine the chance of the event with its speed; age, cohort and survey are near-collinear and the age adjustment is described inconsistently; income and education measured at interview are adjusted for; the three-way interaction coefficients are not shown; no correction for many tests.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Response rates 90% (NLAES) and 81% (NESARC), with weights adjusting for the designs.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is moderate risk. The descriptive numbers (ages at first drink by sex and cohort; who ever became dependent or entered treatment) come from large probability samples with good response and a standard interview. The analytic conclusions about telescoping are weaker than the data handling: every timing is recalled; the main estimand (hazard among all at risk) is not the quantity telescoping refers to (speed among those who reach the landmark); the youngest cohort is observed only to age 27; and several table and text values disagree. The paper may be cited for the absence of the full telescoping pattern in two US general-population surveys of US-born adults aged 18–57 interviewed in 1991–1992 and 2001–2002, for women's later first drink and its narrowing across cohorts, and for men's higher hazards of dependence and treatment; it should not be cited as showing that men progress faster from first drink to dependence among people who become dependent, and its treatment figures should be cited with the inconsistencies noted.

key_findings.finding: Pooled sample of 53,238 US-born adults aged 18–57 from NLAES (1991–1992, response 90%) and NESARC (2001–2002, response 81%): cohort 1 (born 1974–1983) 5,845, cohort 2 (1964–1973) 13,555, cohort 3 (1954–1963) 16,329, cohort 4 (1944–1953) 12,906, cohort 5 (1934–1943) 4,603. A general-population sample; timing of every landmark was recalled at one interview.
key_findings.locator: Method › Sources of Data, 1st–4th paragraphs; Method › Measures

key_findings.finding: Mean age at first drink, men vs women (Table 1): overall 17.8 (SE 0.03) vs 19.0 (SE 0.04) years; cohort 1 17.1 vs 17.5; cohort 2 17.2 vs 17.7; cohort 3 17.5 vs 18.5; cohort 4 18.4 vs 20.5; cohort 5 19.1 vs 22.1. Women were older at first drink in every cohort (t from −2.80, p=0.007, in cohort 1 to −19.58, p<0.001, in cohort 4); the gap narrowed from 3.0 years in the oldest to 0.4 years in the youngest cohort (editors' subtraction).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Alcohol use initiation

key_findings.finding: Hazard of a first drink, men vs women (Cox, Table 2): cohort 5 2.19 (95% CI 2.01–2.39), cohort 4 2.01 (1.91–2.12), cohort 3 1.62 (1.55–1.70), cohort 2 1.50 (1.43–1.57), cohort 1 1.50 (1.37–1.64); cohort-by-gender interaction F=16.7, df=4, p<0.01, read by the authors as a narrowing gender gap; three-way interaction with time F=0.10, df=6, p=0.84.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and footnote b; Results › Multivariate Results: Two-Way Interaction of Gender and Birth Cohort on Event Hazard

key_findings.finding: Mean time from first drink to dependence among people who became dependent, men vs women (Table 1): overall 5.8 (SE 0.12) vs 5.6 (SE 0.15) years, ratio 1.04, not significant; cohort 1 2.8 vs 3.1; cohort 2 4.2 vs 3.7 (women shorter, t=2.36, p=0.02); cohort 3 6.4 vs 5.5 (not marked significant); cohort 4 7.9 vs 8.6; cohort 5 10.4 vs 11.8.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Time from initiation to dependence onset
key_findings.note: These conditional means are the closest analogue to the treatment-sample measure of telescoping; the authors set them aside because mean durations depend on age at interview.

key_findings.finding: Time from first drink to dependence among all 38,309 lifetime drinkers: survival curves fell faster for men in every cohort (log-rank 46.7, 69.6, 110.8, 181.8 and 36.3 for cohorts 1–5, all p<0.01); Cox hazard ratios, men vs women, 1.56 (1.35–1.79), 1.36 (1.23–1.50), 1.46 (1.33–1.62), 1.79 (1.58–2.02) and 1.71 (1.34–2.20) for cohorts 1–5. The authors read this as men becoming dependent at a faster rate, contrary to telescoping.
key_findings.locator: Results › Bivariate Results: Survival Curves by Gender and Birth Cohort › Gender difference (Figure 2); Table 2
key_findings.note: A hazard among all drinkers mixes the chance of ever becoming dependent with the speed of progression; see the interpretation gap.

key_findings.finding: Three-way interaction of cohort, gender and time for time from first drink to dependence: F=54.08 (Table 2: 54.1), df=6, p<0.01; its direction is 'data not shown' and is described as men having a shorter time to dependence than women, and than men in earlier cohorts, in more recent cohorts. Three-way interactions were not significant for first drink or for time to treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Multivariate Results: Three-Way Interaction of Gender, Birth Cohort, and Time to Event on Event Hazard; Table 2 footnote c

key_findings.finding: Time from dependence to first treatment among people with dependence (N=8,564): men had a shorter time in cohorts 2, 3 and 4 (log-rank 15.1, 19.5 and 7.0, p<0.01), no difference in cohorts 1 and 5; Cox hazard ratios, men vs women, 1.16 (0.77–1.76), 1.55 (1.22–1.96), 1.42 (1.16–1.73), 1.20 (0.91–1.58), 1.38 (0.84–2.26) for cohorts 1–5; no cohort-by-gender (F=0.92, p=0.46) or three-way (F=0.02, p=0.98) interaction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Bivariate Results: Survival Curves by Gender and Birth Cohort › Gender difference (Figure 3); Table 2 and footnote d

key_findings.finding: Mean time from dependence to first treatment among people treated after dependence onset, men vs women (Table 1): overall 7.0 (SE 0.28) vs 6.1 (SE 0.37) years, ratio 1.15, p<0.05 (women shorter); cohort 5 23.5 vs 19.4 years (t=3.2, p=0.002); no significant difference in cohorts 1–4.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort › Time from dependence onset to first treatment utilization
key_findings.note: The overall means cannot be reconciled with the cohort rows (reporting issue 2); cite the cohort-5 comparison rather than the overall one.

key_findings.finding: Main effects in the Cox models: men had a higher hazard of first drink (F=1,536.9), of dependence among drinkers (F=223.2) and of treatment among people with dependence (F=22.7), each df=1, p<0.001; later cohorts had higher hazards of first drink (F=82.95, df=4) and of dependence among drinkers (F=227.7, df=4), with no cohort effect on treatment. In life tables, each successively younger cohort progressed faster from first drink to dependence (pairwise p<0.01 in both sexes), while the youngest cohort was later to first drink than cohort 2 (log-rank 37.7 in men; the results in women are described as analogous).
key_findings.locator: Results › Multivariate Results: Effect of Birth Cohort and Gender › Gender difference and Cohort effect; Results › Bivariate Results: Survival Curves by Gender and Birth Cohort › Cohort effect

key_findings.finding: 24.6% of people with alcohol dependence in these data had ever used any type of alcohol treatment; the authors say this left too little power to detect small cohort differences in treatment.
key_findings.note: Table 1 counts give 3,056 treated after onset of 8,564 with dependence, about 36% unweighted (editors' arithmetic); the 24.6% may be weighted, which the paper does not say.

key_findings.finding: Recall check: within each birth cohort, the prevalence of dependence beginning at age 25 or later did not differ between respondents interviewed in NLAES and those interviewed 10 years later in NESARC, which the authors take as evidence of limited recall bias; post hoc analyses run separately by survey were described as similar in direction and size.

The authors suggest, as a possibility, that the narrowing gender gap in the overall hazard of dependence reflects protective social factors (for example, social sanctions on women's drinking) that weakened as gender norms shifted; they cite research consistent with changing norms (greater acceptability of women drinking, advertising exposure among adolescent women, cross-national surveys) and state that they know of no formal test of this possibility. They recommend more screening of younger women for alcohol use disorders and further study of the apparent faster progression to dependence in younger men.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 2,634 cohort-1 men in the age-at-first-drink column, more than the 2,553 cohort-1 men in the sample; the column sums agree with the totals, so one of the two cohort-1 figures must be wrong (the corresponding share for cohort-1 women, 1,667 of 3,292, is also out of line with the other cohorts).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1, cohort 1 rows
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of drinkers in the youngest cohort cannot be taken from Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the total-sample mean times from dependence to first treatment (men 7.0, women 6.1 years) cannot be averages of its cohort rows: cohorts 3–5 hold 1,491 of the 2,088 treated men and have means of 14.8–23.5 years, and the printed numbers give about 14.8 years for men and 13.2 for women (editors' arithmetic; survey weights could not plausibly bring this down to 7.0). The total row's ratio (1.15) matches its own means.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1, time from dependence to treatment column
reporting_issues.consequence: The overall finding that women reached treatment sooner (6.1 vs 7.0 years, p<0.05) should not be cited until the discrepancy is resolved; the cohort-specific rows are internally consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: Analysed numbers differ without explanation: the Table 1 counts of drinkers sum to 38,812, against 38,309 lifetime drinkers in Figure 2 and Table 2; Table 1 lists 7,752 people with a time from first drink to dependence, against 8,564 people with dependence (after excluding 258) in Figure 3 and Table 2.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1; Figure 2 and 3 titles; Table 2 column heads
reporting_issues.consequence: Missing data on onset ages, and how they were handled, are not described; the denominators of the conditional means and of the survival analyses are not the same people.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance markers in Table 1 disagree with the text: for age at first drink in cohort 1 the text gives t=−2.80, p=0.007, while Table 1 marks p<0.001; for time to treatment in cohort 5 the text gives t=3.2, p=0.002, while Table 1 marks p<0.001. The cohort-3 difference in time to dependence (6.4 vs 5.5 years, SEs 0.21 and 0.31) is not marked although the printed means and SEs give t of about 2.4 (editors' approximation ignoring within-design covariance; the same approximation gives 2.2 for cohort 2, where the paper reports 2.36).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 1 footnotes c and d; Results › Bivariate Results: Mean Time to Event by Gender and Birth Cohort
reporting_issues.consequence: Small, but the cohort-3 point bears on telescoping: by the printed numbers women who became dependent may also have done so faster in cohort 3.

reporting_issues.issue: The cohort-by-gender interaction for time from first drink to dependence is given as F=2.8 (text) and F=2.83 (Figure 2 legend), p=0.03, but as F=2.51, p=0.04 in the Table 2 footnote.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Results › Multivariate Results: Two-Way Interaction; Figure 2 legend; Table 2 footnote c
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the interaction is significant in all versions.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the men-to-women hazard ratio for a first drink in cohort 4 as 2.10; Table 2 gives 2.01 (1.91–2.12).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Results › Multivariate Results: Two-Way Interaction, 1st paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Transposed digits; use the table value.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say age was evaluated as a confounder but not kept in the final models; the Results and the Table 2 footnote say the models controlled for age.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Method › Statistical Analysis, 5th paragraph; Results › Multivariate Results; Table 2 footnote a
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which model produced the hazard ratios; with age, cohort and survey near-collinear, the choice matters for the cohort estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The three-way interaction tests are given 6 degrees of freedom, which does not match a five-level cohort by two-level gender by time term (4 df if time is continuous); how time entered the interaction is not described, and the coefficients are not shown.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Table 2 footnotes b–d; Method › Statistical Analysis, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's claim that men progress faster especially in younger cohorts cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that, on mean times as well as survival curves, women had neither a shorter time to dependence nor a shorter time to first treatment, but Table 1 shows significantly shorter mean times in women to dependence in cohort 2 and to treatment overall and in cohort 5.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary in the Discussion is stronger than the table; the evidence against telescoping rests on the hazard analyses, not on the conditional means.

disagreements.first_pass: The authors attribute narrowing gender gaps to weakening social restraints on women's drinking, citing changing norms and advertising exposure, and state that they know of no formal test of this explanation; they recommend more screening of younger women for alcohol use disorders and further study of faster progression in younger men.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 276, corrected: the authors do not attribute the narrowing gap to weaker social restraints; they say the convergence is consistent with the possibility that protective social factors diminished, list supporting research and note that no formal test exists; write 'suggest, as a possibility', not 'attribute'. Recommendations (7th paragraph) confirmed.
